issues.description: The problem statement (and UML) requires addGuestStudents(int, String) — i.e., the method should accept an int and a String reason — but the solution implementation provides addGuestStudents(int) with only a single int parameter. This mismatch between the specification and the reference implementation can confuse students about the expected method signature and cause tests or usage examples that rely on the reason parameter to fail.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the solution implementation match the specification by changing the method signature to addGuestStudents(int numberOfNewGuestStudents, String reason) and update its body to add numberOfNewGuestStudents to numberOfGuestStudents (and optionally record or log the provided reason). Alternatively, if the reason parameter is not intended, update the problem statement and UML to specify addGuestStudents(int) consistently.

issues.description: The problem statement and UML require an addGuestStudents(int, String) method that accepts a number and a reason, but the solution implements addGuestStudents(int) (single parameter) and the template only contains a TODO. This mismatch in the method signature (parameter count and intended parameter 'reason') creates a mapping/confusion between the requirement and the provided implementation: students will look for a two-parameter method as specified in the task but find only a one-parameter implementation in the solution/template.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the method signatures consistent. Either update the solution and template to implement the two-parameter method as specified: public void addGuestStudents(int numberOfNewGuestStudents, String reason) (and handle/store/log the reason), or change the problem statement/UML to require only a single int parameter. Preferred fix: implement public void addGuestStudents(int numberOfNewGuestStudents, String reason) in both template and solution so the code matches the stated requirements.
